title: RCA's expectations and the first session
summary: RCA expected nostalgia; Doodletown Fifers and A&R man Dave Kapp's fight for it.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Originally was it just intended to be a studio--

At that point it was. We just did those dates and it was sold as being better--bigger and better. It wasn't any longer just Miller, it was Goodman plus Miller. That's what they thought they were going to get.
So they didn't think they were going to get anything that was unusal, it was a nostalgia thing.
They were pretty sure that they could sell it by the name,
and if it sounded that way, they figured that one half of the record would sound like Benny and the other half like Miller. And they really didn't want what they got.
How did you manage to get them to record what you wanted to do?
They had to do that because they didn't know beforehand what it was going to be.
They just assumed that because you had written for Goodman and Bill had written for Miller that that's what they were going to get?

So we came in and did "Doodletown Fifers" and a couple of other things, about four things we had to do the first session and Dave Capp was the A and R man; he was sort of stuck with it at this point. The sales department didn't want any part of that and Dave had to fight for it.

So eventually it was released, and when it was released the disc jockeys picked right up on it and we became one of the proverbial "overnight things", which I wish hadn't happened, because it put us out on the road, where we immediately began to lose money that we didn't have in the first place. Although we waited a year to do it.
